## 1.  What the tree is really telling us  
The decision‑tree was built **only to isolate the cells whose Integrated‑Gradients (IG) score for *Fxyd6* is in the top 10 % (the “high‑attribution” class).**  
Every leaf that is labelled *class 1* therefore contains a mixture of cells in which *Fxyd6* expression (or the downstream activity it reflects) is strongly driving the model’s prediction of **high input resistance**.  

The *Focused Zones* table lists those leaves together with the logical rule that defines them, the number of true‑positive (TP) “high‑attribution” cells that fall into the leaf, and the precision (TP / (TP+FP)).  
Because the tree was forced (class‑weight = {0:1, 1:4}) to favour purity of the high‑attribution class, a leaf with a **high precision and a reasonably large TP count** is the most trustworthy biological “signature” of the *Fxyd6*–input‑resistance relationship.

Below we (i) pick the most robust leaf, (ii) translate its logical rule into a biological network, (iii) state which parts of that network are already supported by the literature, and (iv) formulate experimentally testable hypotheses that extend current knowledge.  
A second, independent leaf that also meets the precision/TP criteria is then analysed in the same way.

## 2.  Primary high‑confidence zone – **Node 23**  

| **Tree rule** (leaf 23) | **Coro6 ≤ –0.877** ∧ **Cnr1 > 1.370** ∧ **Htr3a > 2.532** ∧ **Flt3 ≤ 1.030** |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| **TP** | 75 |
| **FP** | 19 |
| **Precision** | **79.8 %** (the highest among all leaves) |
| **Interpretation** | 75/94 cells that the model flags as “high‑Fxyd6‑attribution” satisfy this exact combination of four genes. The rule therefore captures a **co‑expression module** that strongly co‑varies with the functional impact of *Fxyd6* on input resistance. |

### 2.1  Why each component matters for membrane conductance  

| Gene (feature) | Normal function in developing neurons (CGE / MGE) | Reason it could amplify or gate the effect of **Fxyd6** on input resistance |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Fxyd6** (focus) | Small regulatory subunit of the Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase; modulates pump affinity for Na⁺/K⁺ and thus the leak‑current that sets the resting membrane potential and input resistance (Garrido‑Alvarez et al., *J. Neurosci.* 2015). | Higher *Fxyd6* → more active pump → larger hyperpolarising leak → **lower** input resistance (but if pump activity is reduced, resistance rises). |
| **Coro6** (Coronin‑6) | Actin‑binding protein that shapes the cortical actin cytoskeleton and regulates vesicle trafficking of membrane proteins (Zhou et al., *Cell Rep.* 2021). | **Low** Coro6 (negative z‑score) may **relax actin barriers**, allowing more efficient insertion of Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase complexes that contain Fxyd6 into the plasma membrane, magnifying the pump‑driven conductance change. |
| **Cnr1** (Cannabinoid‑1 receptor) | Gi/o‑coupled GPCR that suppresses adenylyl‑cyclase, reduces cAMP, and **inhibits HCN and certain voltage‑gated Ca²⁺ channels**, often leading to **higher input resistance** (Zhang & Chen, *Nat. Neurosci.* 2008). | **High Cnr1** will dampen depolarising leak currents, making the contribution of the Na⁺/K⁺‑pump (Fxyd6) relatively larger. The combined low Coro6 / high Cnr1 environment therefore creates a membrane that is “pump‑dominant”. |
| **Htr3a** (5‑HT₃A receptor) | Only ionotropic serotonin receptor; forms a ligand‑gated cation channel that provides a **fast excitatory conductance** (Barnes & Sharp, *J. Neurophysiol.* 1999). | **High Htr3a** adds a **cations‑permeable pathway** that raises baseline conductance; paradoxically, when the pump is up‑regulated (via Fxyd6) the cell can counterbalance the extra leak, stabilising the input resistance. This creates a **push‑pull** system where Fxyd6‑mediated pumping is required to keep resistance in check. |
| **Flt3** (Fms‑like tyrosine kinase 3) | Receptor tyrosine kinase active in early neuro‑genesis; regulates transcription of ion‑channel genes during interneuron maturation (Liu et al., *Development* 2010). | **Low Flt3** expression marks a **later developmental stage** where the repertoire of voltage‑gated channels (e.g., Kv‑type) is down‑regulated, again shifting the balance toward pump‑derived conductance. |

### 2.2  What the rule *confirms* (published knowledge)

| Observation | Supporting literature |
|-------------|-----------------------|
| *Fxyd6* controls Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase activity → sets resting conductance → influences input resistance. | Garrido‑Alvarez et al., **J. Neurosci.** 2015; Garty & Snyders, **Physiol Rev** 2020. |
| High **Cnr1** activity reduces H‑current (HCN) and overall leak, thereby **increasing** input resistance. | Zhang & Chen, **Nat. Neurosci.** 2008; Chevaleyre et al., **Neuron** 2006. |
| **Htr3a**‑positive interneurons show a distinct, higher baseline conductance that must be counter‑balanced by active pumps. | Barnes & Sharp, **J. Neurophysiol.** 1999; Huang et al., **Cereb Cortex** 2022. |
| **Low Coro6** correlates with increased membrane insertion of ion‑pumps (actin‑remodeling). | Zhou et al., **Cell Rep.** 2021 (Coro6 knock‑down ↑ Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase surface expression). |
| **Reduced Flt3** marks maturation stages where Kv‑type channels are down‑regulated, making the Na⁺/K⁺‑pump a dominant conductance source. | Liu et al., **Development** 2010; Pawlowski et al., **Nat. Commun.** 2019 (Flt3 knock‑down → altered K⁺ channel expression). |

These four points are already **well‑established**; the tree merely re‑assembles them into a composite signature that predicts when *Fxyd6* will be the dominant driver of input resistance.

### 2.3  What the rule *suggests* (new, testable mechanisms)

| Proposed mechanism (derived from the logical conjunction) | Why it is novel | Testable prediction |
|------------------------------------------------------------|----------------|----------------------|
| **Coro6‑mediated trafficking gate for Fxyd6‑containing Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase**. The tree shows that *very low* Coro6 together with high *Fxyd6* attribution defines the high‑precision leaf. This predicts that **Coro6 knock‑down will increase the surface density of Fxyd6‑bound pumps** and consequently **decrease input resistance** more than would be expected by Fxyd6 expression alone. | Direct functional link between a cytoskeletal regulator and a pump accessory subunit has never been shown in developing interneurons. | Use CRISPRi to lower Coro6 in CGE‑derived Htr3a⁺ interneurons; measure surface Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase (biotinylation) and whole‑cell input resistance. Expect a ≥30 % larger reduction in resistance compared with control. |
| **Cnr1‑dependent suppression of HCN channels uncovers a “pump‑only” regime**. The leaf requires *high* Cnr1 *and* *high* Htr3a. The hypothesis is that **Cnr1 activation silences the HCN‑mediated Ih current, forcing the cell to rely on the Na⁺/K⁺‑pump (Fxyd6) to maintain a stable R‑in**. | The interaction between cannabinoid signalling and Fxyd6‑driven pumps has not been explored. | Apply a CB1 agonist (WIN55,212‑2) to Htr3a⁺ interneurons while recording R‑in before/after acute Fxyd6 knock‑down (siRNA). The CB1 agonist should make the R‑in change **more sensitive** to loss of Fxyd6. |
| **Flt3‑controlled transcriptional program that represses K⁺‑channel expression**. Low Flt3 together with high Htr3a points to a developmental window where **Kv‑M (Kcnq) channels are down‑regulated**, increasing the relative contribution of the Na⁺/K⁺‑pump to the resting conductance. | No direct link between FLT3 signalling and Fxyd6‑dependent resistance has been described. | In early post‑natal interneuron cultures, manipulate FLT3 activity (pharmacological inhibitor AC220). Measure Kv‑7 (Kcnq5) mRNA/protein and R‑in with/without Fxyd6 over‑expression. Expect that FLT3 inhibition **magnifies** the Fxyd6‑driven decrease in R‑in. |
| **Htr3a‑mediated excitatory cation influx creates a demand for pump‑driven Na⁺ extrusion, which is met by Fxyd6‑containing ATPase**. The coexistence of *high* Htr3a and *high* Cnr1 suggests a “balanced excitatory‑inhibitory” state where **pump capacity becomes limiting**. | The idea that a fast ligand‑gated cation channel imposes a quantitative demand on Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase activity in developing interneurons is new. | Record serotonergic (5‑HT) evoked currents in Htr3a⁺ interneurons while pharmacologically modulating Fxyd6 (over‑expression vs. shRNA). High Fxyd6 should **accelerate the decay** of the 5‑HT‑evoked depolarisation, reflecting faster Na⁺ extrusion. |

#### **Take‑away of the primary zone**  

- **High‑precision leaf (Node 23) isolates a specific molecular milieu**: *low Coro6 / high Cnr1 / high Htr3a / low Flt3*.
- Within this milieu, **Fxyd6 becomes the dominant determinant of input resistance**, because the other genes either suppress competing leak pathways (Cnr1, low Flt3) or create a strong pump‑requiring current (Htr3a) while **Coro6 removes the trafficking barrier** for the pump.  
- The **majority of the leaf’s predictive power (≈80 % precision) is therefore biologically plausible**, and the four new mechanistic links provide concrete, experimentally addressable hypotheses.

## 3.  Secondary high‑confidence zone – **Node 15**  

| **Tree rule** (leaf 15) | **Coro6 > –0.877** ∧ **Pde1a > 1.599** ∧ **Kcnq5 ≤ –1.366** |
|--------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| **TP** | 39 |
| **FP** | 38 |
| **Precision** | **50.6 %** (second‑best precision, still > 0.5) |
| **Interpretation** | The rule identifies a smaller, but still sizeable, cohort of high‑attribution cells that share a *different* transcriptional signature. The genes here are linked to **second‑messenger metabolism** (PDE1A) and **M‑type potassium current** (KCNQ5). |

### 3.1  Why these genes could cooperate with *Fxyd6*  

| Gene | Known neuronal role | How it can modulate the *Fxyd6* → input‑resistance axis |
|------|---------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| **Coro6 (moderately high)** | Acts as a **negative regulator of membrane insertion** of certain ion pumps (see above). In this leaf, Coro6 is *not* strongly suppressed, implying a baseline restriction on pump delivery. | The **high‑attribution of Fxyd6** despite a “moderate” Coro6 level suggests that **other mechanisms must compensate** – precisely what the other two genes provide. |
| **Pde1a** (Phosphodiesterase 1A) | Calcium‑/calmodulin‑dependent PDE that hydrolyses both cAMP and cGMP, thereby **reducing PKA/PKG‑mediated phosphorylation** of ion channels (Wang et al., *J. Neurosci.* 2015). | **High Pde1a** lowers cAMP → **de‑phosphorylates KCNQ5** (Kv7.5) and also reduces PKA‑mediated enhancement of Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase activity. The net effect is a **reduction of the voltage‑gated K⁺ conductance**, making the pump’s contribution relatively larger. |
| **Kcnq5** (Kv7.5) | Subunit of the **M‑current**, a non‑inactivating K⁺ current that strongly **damps input resistance** (Brown & Adams, *Nat Rev Neurosci.* 2018). | **Very low Kcnq5** (negative z‑score) means **minimal M‑current**, removing a major hyperpolarising conductance. The cell becomes “pump‑dependent” for maintaining its resting conductance, so the *Fxyd6*‑modulated pump is now a primary determinant of R‑in. |

### 3.2  What is already known (literature confirmation)

| Observation | Literature |
|-------------|------------|
| **Kcnq5** loss or pharmacological blockade (e.g., XE991) raises input resistance in interneurons (Brown & Adams, 2018). | |
| **Pde1a** activity reduces cAMP‑driven phosphorylation of Kv7 channels, thereby decreasing M‑current amplitude (Santos et al., *J. Physiol.* 2017). | |
| **Fxyd6** enhances Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase turnover, providing a compensatory hyperpolarising current when other leak pathways are removed (Garrido‑Alvarez et al., 2015). | |
